scenario_stem:
Oakhurst Precision Tools is a private limited company that manufactures precision measuring instruments in the industrial town of Brannock. Founded in 2011, it employs 45 production workers and sells instruments to engineering firms across Country X, generating $950,000 in annual revenue last year. Its customers include toolmakers and machine-tool shops in three other provinces, and several export buyers in coastal industrial regions.

The directors want to install automated calibration machines costing $220,000 to raise output by 30% and cut unit costs, shifting the objective from steady profit to rapid growth. Trade union representatives warn that automation could eliminate 18 of the 45 jobs, and workers have voted to oppose the plan. The two owners disagree on whether to protect jobs or pursue growth this year.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'stakeholder'.
questions.model_answer: Any individual, group or organisation that has an interest in, or is affected by, the activities and decisions of a business. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Any individual, group or organisation with an interest in a business
Affected by the business's activities and decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the owners and the workers at Oakhurst may have conflicting objectives over the automation plan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Owners want to reduce costs and increase output [k], because the $220,000 machines would raise output by 30% and could win larger orders from engineering firms across Country X [app]. Reason 2: Workers want job security and stable wages [k], because the union warns that 18 of the 45 production roles could disappear if automation goes ahead [app].

knowledge_max_2: Owners seek lower costs and higher profit or growth
Workers seek job security and fair treatment
application_max_2: $220,000 machines would raise output by 30%
18 of the 45 production roles at risk of elimination

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Oakhurst could manage the conflict between the owners and the workers.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Oakhurst could consult with the workers and their union before deciding [k], for example holding meetings about the $220,000 plan and the 18 at-risk roles [app], so employees feel heard and may accept retraining instead of resisting the change [an]. Point 2: Oakhurst could retrain or redeploy affected workers into new roles [k], offering the 18 workers training to operate or maintain the new calibration machines [app], which would reduce redundancies and keep skilled staff available for the 30% output increase [an].

knowledge_max_2: Consultation and negotiation with workers and the union
Retraining or redeployment of affected staff
application_max_2: Meetings to discuss the $220,000 plan and the 18 at-risk roles
Training to operate the new machines for the 30% output increase
analysis_max_2: Consultation builds trust and reduces resistance
Retraining retains skills and reduces redundancies

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhurst should approve the $220,000 investment in automated calibration machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for approving the investment is that the new machines would raise output by 30% [k], cutting unit costs for Oakhurst Precision Tools and helping it win larger orders from toolmakers across Country X [app], which could protect the business's survival and fund future growth [an]. However, one argument against is that automation could eliminate 18 of the 45 jobs [k], harming employee morale and creating bitter conflict with the trade union [app], which may damage productivity and undermine the very growth the owners want [an]. Overall, Oakhurst should not approve the machines immediately [eval]; it should first negotiate retraining and redeployment with the union, then approve the $220,000 investment in a phased programme that keeps most staff while still achieving the 30% output target [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automation raises output and cuts unit costs
Automation risks job losses and employee resistance
application_max_2: $220,000 cost against a 30% output increase
18 of the 45 jobs at risk
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs support survival and future growth
Job losses could damage morale, productivity and union relations
evaluation_max_2: Weighs automation benefits against worker welfare
Reaches a justified judgement favouring a phased, negotiated approach

scenario_stem:
Linden & Locke Joinery is a two-partner joinery business in the market town of Calder. Founded in 2019, it employs 7 craftspeople making bespoke doors and staircases for housebuilders. For its first three years the partners focused on survival, keeping costs low and accepting small orders to build a reputation that buyers value for handmade finish and reliable delivery.

Last year Linden & Locke generated $260,000 in revenue and a profit of $32,000. The partners now disagree over the objective. Partner A wants rapid growth: hiring 5 more staff and opening a second workshop. Partner B wants to stay small, protect the $32,000 annual profit and avoid $1,800 of monthly repayments on a $70,000 expansion loan. Housebuilding in Calder is recovering after a slow period.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'survival' as a business objective.
questions.model_answer: Continuing to stay in business and keep trading, especially in the early years or during difficult conditions, rather than seeking profit or growth. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Continuing to trade and remain in business
Prioritising staying in business over profit or growth, often in early years or hard times

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a new business may set survival as its main objective.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A new business may lack capital and a steady customer base to absorb losses [k], and Linden & Locke spent its first three years keeping costs low and accepting small orders to build a reputation [app]. Reason 2: Survival allows the owners to reinvest everything the business earns instead of taking profit out [k], which is how the partners reached $260,000 of revenue last year with a modest $32,000 profit [app].

knowledge_max_2: Limited capital and uncertain customer demand in early years
Focus on reinvestment and building reputation rather than profit-taking
application_max_2: First three years spent keeping costs low and accepting small orders
$260,000 revenue and $32,000 profit achieved last year

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Linden & Locke of changing its objective from survival to growth.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Growth would let the business serve more customers and raise revenue [k], since hiring 5 more staff and opening a second workshop would increase capacity well beyond the current 7 craftspeople [app], raising sales potential and spreading fixed costs over a higher output [an]. Advantage 2: Growth can improve profit in the long run [k], because $260,000 of revenue produced only $32,000 of profit last year, and extra volume could lift total profit above that level [app], giving both partners a better financial return on their work [an].

knowledge_max_2: Growth increases capacity, revenue and market presence

application_max_2: 5 more staff and a second workshop beyond the 7 craftspeople
$260,000 revenue produced only $32,000 of profit
analysis_max_2: Higher capacity spreads fixed costs over more output
Higher volume lifts long-run profit for both partners

questions.question_text: Do you think Linden & Locke should change its objective from survival to rapid growth? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for changing the objective is that growth would raise capacity [k]: hiring 5 staff and opening a second workshop could lift revenue well above $260,000 and total profit beyond the $32,000 earned last year [app], giving the partners a stronger market position against larger joinery firms as housebuilding recovers in Calder [an]. However, one argument against is that rapid growth strains a small business [k]: the $70,000 expansion loan would add $1,800 of monthly repayments even if orders are slow [app], which could consume the modest $32,000 profit and put the business back at risk [an]. Overall, the partners should change to a growth objective but expand gradually rather than all at once [eval], financing the second workshop from retained profit first and taking the loan only if the order book justifies it [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Growth objective raises capacity and competitiveness
Rapid growth adds debt and financial risk
application_max_2: 5 staff and a second workshop to lift revenue above $260,000

analysis_max_2: Extra capacity lets the business win more housebuilding orders
Fixed loan repayments could exhaust profit if demand stalls
evaluation_max_2: Weighs growth opportunity against debt risk
Reaches a justified judgement favouring gradual, staged expansion

scenario_stem:
Marisol Spice Co is a social enterprise that imports and blends authentic spices in the port city of Barra. Founded in 2016 by Priya Raman, the business employs 14 young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, paying them the national living wage and providing accredited training. It generates $380,000 in annual sales through local shops, markets and an online store, and donates $20,000 a year to a community kitchen.

Priya is considering converting Marisol Spice into a private limited company focused on maximising profit. New investors would expect a $45,000 annual dividend and may pressure the board to cut the $28,000 training programme and the $20,000 donation. Profit could be reinvested to open a second shop, but the social mission may be diluted. Priya must decide whether growth justifies giving up the mission-driven approach.

questions.model_answer: A business that trades to achieve social or environmental objectives, using its profits to benefit the community rather than solely to maximise returns for owners. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A business that trades goods or services

Reason 2: To put profits back into the community [k], the business donates $20,000 a year to a community kitchen rather than maximising owner returns [app].

knowledge_max_2: Uses trade to address social problems such as unemployment

application_max_2: 14 young people employed at the national living wage
$20,000 a year donated to a community kitchen

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Investors may pressure the business to cut its social programmes [k], because new shareholders would expect a $45,000 annual dividend [app], which could force Marisol to drop the $28,000 training programme or the $20,000 donation to balance its books [an]. Problem 2: The business may lose the mission-driven identity that attracts customers [k], since authentic blending and community support help generate $380,000 of annual sales [app], so abandoning the social mission could reduce revenue and damage the brand [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shareholders expect dividends and pressure management to prioritise them

questions.question_text: Do you think Marisol Spice should convert to a private limited company focused on maximising profit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for converting is that new investors would inject share capital [k], funding a second shop and growing revenue well beyond $380,000 a year [app], which could create more jobs and training places for disadvantaged young people [an]. However, one argument against is that a profit-maximising company would have to pay the $45,000 dividend [k], putting pressure to cut the $28,000 training programme and the $20,000 community donation [app], which would undermine the very mission that keeps its customers loyal [an]. Overall, Marisol should not convert to a profit-maximising company [eval]; it should raise smaller sums through retained profit, grants and community fundraising instead, opening the second shop gradually while keeping its social mission and its 14 young workers [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Weighs growth funding against mission dilution
Reaches a justified judgement favouring retained profit and grants

scenario_stem:
Bluepine Sawmill Ltd operates a timber sawmill at the edge of Kestrelwick village, cutting and finishing planks for builders across the region. Founded in 2009, it employs 38 workers and generates $720,000 in annual revenue, running double shifts five days a week, six in peak season. It is the village's second-largest employer after the school.

Neighbouring residents have complained about noise, dust and up to 55 logging truck movements a week. The Country X environmental agency warns Bluepine that it must fit dust extractors costing $60,000 and cap truck movements at 30 per week by next year, or face a $25,000 fine. The owners want to keep output high to protect profit, while the village council demands immediate action. Residents say the dust settles on gardens and trucks damage road verges.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'stakeholder conflict'.
questions.model_answer: A disagreement between stakeholder groups that have different objectives or interests in a business's decisions. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A disagreement between stakeholder groups

Reason 2: The community wants a safe and quiet living environment [k], objecting to the noise, the dust and the 55 logging truck movements passing through the village each week [app].

questions.model_answer: Point 1: To avoid financial penalties and possible closure [k], the agency warned that a $25,000 fine would follow if the mill failed to act [app], which would wipe out a chunk of profit and could threaten the jobs of the 38 workers [an]. Point 2: To protect its reputation and its licence to operate [k], fitting $60,000 of dust extractors and capping trucks at 30 per week would satisfy the village council [app], reducing complaints, avoiding legal action and rebuilding trust with residents [an].

However, one argument against is that the $60,000 cost is significant for the sawmill [k], and cutting truck movements from 55 to 30 per week could reduce deliveries to builders [app], squeezing profit at a time when timber and wage costs may already be tight [an]. Overall, Bluepine should invest in the dust extractors now [eval], spreading the cost and agreeing a phased truck cap with the council, because the fine, the loss of trust and possible closure far outweigh the short-term cost [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Weighs compliance costs against fines and closure risk

scenario_stem:
Kelpie Bay Hotel is a private limited company on the coast of Country X, with 40 shareholders and 65 employees. It is a popular wedding and conference venue for the region, with 78 rooms and a busy restaurant. Last year it made a profit of $180,000.

The board of directors wants to keep $150,000 of the profit to refurbish guest rooms, the restaurant kitchen and the booking system, changing the objective from survival to growth and aiming to raise market share from 9% to 12%. Most shareholders want a larger cash dividend this year instead. A minority of shareholders who are also managers support the refurbishment plan, believing it will lift long-term returns. They point to the hotel's ageing decor and slow Wi-Fi, which are currently losing weddings to rival hotels nearby.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the shareholders and the managers may have conflicting objectives over the use of last year's profit.

Reason 2: The board wants to reinvest profit to achieve growth [k], planning to keep $150,000 of the $180,000 profit for refurbishment to lift market share from 9% to 12% [app].

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Refurbishment could increase revenue and market share [k], by offering new rooms, a faster booking system and modern facilities that attract more wedding and conference guests [app], which would raise future profit and strengthen the hotel against rivals [an]. Benefit 2: Reinvestment supports the growth objective [k], helping Kelpie Bay raise market share from 9% to 12% over the next two years [app], which would increase the business's value and ultimately allow bigger dividends for shareholders later [an].

However, one argument against is that withholding reinvestment would delay the refurbishment [k], costing the hotel the chance to raise market share from 9% to 12% with the $150,000 of planned improvements [app], weakening future profit and share value for everyone [an]. Overall, Kelpie Bay should reinvest the majority of the profit and pay only a modest dividend [eval], for example keeping dividends small this year while the refurbishment lifts revenue and share value, balancing both groups of shareholders fairly [eval].

scenario_stem:
Averton Foods Plc operates 12 supermarkets across the eastern region of Country X, employing 480 staff and generating $28 million in annual revenue. Its basket covers everyday groceries, fresh produce and household goods for low- and middle-income families. Its stores range from town-centre branches to two large out-of-town superstores.

Shareholders have demanded a profit margin of 8% this year, up from 6% last year. The board plans to raise prices on 600 essential grocery lines and cut 40 jobs to reach the target. Consumers have reacted angrily: a customer association is calling for a boycott, weekly sales have fallen 9% since the announcement, and the government has warned Averton over misleading 'value' promotions. Union representatives say proposed job cuts would overload remaining checkout staff.

questions.model_answer: The financial surplus remaining from revenue after all costs have been deducted; the reward for taking the risk of operating a business. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Surplus of revenue over all costs
Reward for taking the risk of running a business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Averton Foods' shareholders want a higher profit margin.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shareholders want a better return on their investment [k], which is why they have demanded the profit margin rise from 6% to 8% this year [app]. Reason 2: Higher profit strengthens the business and funds growth [k], supporting $28 million of annual revenue and the owners' plans to refurbish the 12 regional stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher returns for shareholders
Retained profit funds growth and business strength
application_max_2: Profit margin demanded to rise from 6% to 8%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by raising prices on 600 essential grocery lines and cutting 40 staff.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Customers may shop with rivals instead [k], which is already visible in weekly sales falling 9% after the announcement [app], so revenue could shrink and the 8% margin target could become harder, not easier, to reach [an]. Problem 2: Service quality may fall for shoppers [k], because cutting 40 of the 480 staff leaves fewer checkouts and less help on the shop floor [app], damaging customer loyalty and pushing more shoppers to competitors [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices drive customers to rivals
Fewer staff reduce service quality

questions.model_answer: One argument for raising prices is that it protects the profit margin shareholders want [k], lifting it from 6% to 8% on $28 million of annual revenue and funding dividends [app], which would reward investors and keep share capital in the business [an]. However, one argument against is that higher prices on essentials hurt low-income consumers [k], and sales have already fallen 9% since the announcement while the government has warned over misleading 'value' promotions [app], which could trigger legal action, further lost sales and lasting brand damage [an]. Overall, Averton should not raise prices on essential lines [eval]; it should hold prices, cut waste and improve stock control instead, keeping customers loyal even if the margin stays near 6% for another year [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ferryhill Boatyard is a small private limited company in the fishing port of Dunraven, employing 16 boatbuilders and repairers. It generates $340,000 in annual revenue, mainly refitting fishing vessels for commercial operators, and its two hoists and workshop are busy in summer and quiet in winter. For the last five years its objective was profit, and it paid modest dividends while building a reputation for reliable work.

This year a storm destroyed the harbour's main slipway, and three major contracts worth $120,000 were cancelled. The yard needs $90,000 to repair the slipway and faces rising timber and steel prices. Insurers have not yet confirmed how much of the storm damage they will cover. The owner now wants to switch the objective from profit to survival until the slipway is rebuilt and contracts return.

Disadvantage 2: Survival can damage employee morale and dividends [k], as the 16 boatbuilders may face reduced hours or pay while the slipway is rebuilt [app], which could push skilled staff to leave for other yards [an].

However, one argument against is that focusing only on survival could hollow out the business [k], because holding back reinvestment and cutting hours may push the 16 skilled boatbuilders to rival yards [app], destroying the yard's ability to win contracts once it recovers [an]. scenario_stem:
Ravenscar Woollen Mill is a private limited company in the market town of Hesledon, employing 120 full-time workers in weaving and finishing cloth. It generates $2.4 million in annual revenue and is the town's largest employer; the council estimates the mill contributes $310,000 a year in local business rates and wages. Ravenscar cloth is sold to clothing makers across Country X and abroad.

The owners want to relocate production to a region 400 km away, claiming labour savings of $180,000 a year, or possibly close and sell the site. The government has offered a $150,000 grant and tax incentives to keep the factory in Hesledon, but only if at least 100 jobs are retained for five years. The town council urges acceptance. Local suppliers fear losing their biggest customer. The union wants strict job and wage conditions attached to any grant.

scenario_stem:
Sable & Stone Leatherworks is a partnership producing handmade leather belts and bags in the city of Torvale. Founded in 2015 by two partners, it employs 9 craftspeople and generates $190,000 in annual revenue, shared as $54,000 of annual profit. The partners take turns cutting, stitching and finishing orders for boutiques and online customers.

Partner 1 wants to change the objective from steady profit to growth: borrow $80,000, repaid at $1,600 per month over 5 years, to open a second workshop and hire 6 more leatherworkers. Partner 2 worries the debt would eat into the $54,000 profit and wants to keep the safe objective of steady profit with the current 9 craftspeople. Order books are healthy, but wage and leather costs have risen this year. Retailers have asked about a larger, reliable supply of bags.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'business objective'.
questions.model_answer: A specific target or goal that a business sets for the short, medium or long term to guide its decisions and measure its success. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A specific target or goal for the business
Guides decisions and measures success

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the two partners want different objectives for Sable & Stone Leatherworks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The partners have different attitudes to risk [k], with Partner 1 willing to borrow $80,000 to open a second workshop and hire 6 more staff [app]. Reason 2: The partners may have different personal financial goals [k], with Partner 2 preferring to protect the $54,000 annual profit and avoid $1,600 of monthly repayments [app].

knowledge_max_2: Different attitudes to risk between owners
Different personal financial goals and priorities
application_max_2: $80,000 loan for a second workshop and 6 more staff
$54,000 profit preferred over $1,600 monthly repayments

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Sable & Stone Leatherworks of changing its objective from steady profit to growth.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Growth could raise revenue above $190,000 [k], since a second workshop with 6 extra leatherworkers would allow larger orders for belts and bags [app], increasing total sales and potential profit for both partners [an]. Benefit 2: Growth reduces dependence on one site [k], spreading production across two workshops supplying boutiques and online customers [app], so problems at one site would no longer threaten the whole business [an].

knowledge_max_2: Growth raises capacity, revenue and profit potential
Growth diversifies production risk across sites
application_max_2: Second workshop with 6 extra leatherworkers beyond the current 9 craftspeople
Revenue currently $190,000 with retailers asking for larger supply
analysis_max_2: Larger orders raise sales and profit for both partners
Two sites mean one failure no longer threatens the business

questions.question_text: Do you think Sable & Stone Leatherworks should change its objective from steady profit to growth by borrowing $80,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for changing the objective is that borrowing could unlock growth [k], funding a second workshop and 6 extra staff to lift revenue above the current $190,000 [app], raising capacity and long-run profit beyond the $54,000 earned last year [an]. However, one argument against is that the $1,600 monthly repayments must be paid for 5 years [k], even if the second workshop underperforms or rising wage and leather costs persist [app], which could consume Partner 2's preferred stable income and strain the partnership [an]. Overall, the partners should change only to a cautious growth objective [eval], borrowing $80,000 after a trial scale-up of part-time staff confirms order volumes, with a joint six-monthly review and the right to pause the loan if repayments bite into profit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Borrowing funds growth that raises capacity and long-run profit
Fixed repayments create risk if demand disappoints
application_max_2: $80,000 loan for a second workshop and 6 extra staff beyond $190,000 revenue
$1,600 monthly repayments over 5 years against $54,000 annual profit
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity converts strong order books into revenue and profit
Fixed repayments can strain partnership stability and income
evaluation_max_2: Weighs growth opportunity against fixed-debt risk
Reaches a justified judgement favouring cautious, reviewed expansion

scenario_stem:
Yarrow & Elm Preserves is a community interest company making jams and chutneys in the town of Brindleford. Founded in 2018, it employs 11 workers, eight of whom were long-term unemployed, and generates $210,000 in annual sales. Fruit comes from local orchards, and jars are sold in two farm shops and the town market. Profits of $18,000 a year are reinvested in accredited training and a subsidised cafe. The board keeps all profits in the business rather than distributing them.

The board wants to raise $150,000 to buy modern preserving machinery and win supermarket contracts that could double sales and raise market share from 4% to 7%. Issuing shares to outside investors could provide the $150,000, but new investors would expect dividends and may push the board to drop the training programme, the cafe and subsidised products, changing the community objective into a pure profit objective.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'market share'.
questions.model_answer: The proportion of total sales in a market that is held by one business, usually expressed as a percentage. [2].

knowledge_max_2: The proportion of total sales in a market
Held by one business, usually expressed as a percentage

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Yarrow & Elm Preserves wants to raise its market share from 4%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher market share gives greater market power against rivals [k], and landing supermarket contracts could double Yarrow & Elm's $210,000 of annual sales [app]. Reason 2: Higher market share strengthens the brand's reach and reputation [k], helping the community company win more shelf space than its current 4% slice of the market [app].

knowledge_max_2: Greater market power and competitiveness
Stronger brand reach and reputation
application_max_2: Supermarket contracts could double $210,000 of sales
Current market share is 4% of preserve sales

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Yarrow & Elm may face if it issues shares to outside investors to raise $150,000.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: New investors may demand dividends instead of reinvestment [k], expecting returns from the $150,000 they put in [app], which could force the board to cut the $18,000 a year of community reinvestment [an]. Problem 2: The board may lose control of its social mission [k], as shareholder influence could pressure Yarrow & Elm to drop the training programme for the eight long-term unemployed workers and the subsidised cafe [app], undermining the founding community objective [an].

knowledge_max_2: Outside shareholders expect dividends from profits
Shareholder influence can dilute the social mission
application_max_2: $150,000 share issue against $18,000 a year of community reinvestment
Eight long-term unemployed workers and the subsidised cafe at risk
analysis_max_2: Dividend expectations could force cuts to community spending
Mission dilution undermines the founding community objective

questions.question_text: Do you think Yarrow & Elm Preserves should issue shares to outside investors to raise $150,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for issuing shares is that it provides $150,000 of long-term finance [k], funding modern machinery and supermarket contracts that could double sales and raise market share from 4% to 7% [app], letting the business employ and train more long-term unemployed workers at scale [an]. However, one argument against is that share ownership dilutes the social mission [k], because dividend-seeking investors may push the board to abandon the $18,000 training fund, the cafe and subsidised products [app], converting a community enterprise into a conventional profit-focused business [an]. Overall, Yarrow & Elm should not issue shares to outside investors [eval]; it should raise the $150,000 through retained profits, community fundraising and grants, keeping control of the business and its community objective intact [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Share issues provide long-term growth finance
Share ownership dilutes mission control and adds dividend pressure
application_max_2: $150,000 to double sales and lift market share from 4% to 7%
$18,000 training fund, the cafe and subsidised products at risk from dividends
analysis_max_2: Modern machinery and contracts could scale training and employment
Losing the mission removes the reason the business exists
evaluation_max_2: Weighs growth finance against mission dilution
Reaches a justified judgement favouring retained profit, grants and fundraising
